section.title: The Day of the Lord
section.sectionRationale: Having comforted the grieving with the hope of resurrection, Paul turns to the timing of Christ's return. He will not feed curiosity about dates. Instead he says the Day of the Lord will fall like a thief on a careless world crying peace and security, but believers belong to the light, so they are to live awake, self-controlled, and clothed in faith, love, and hope, resting in the certainty that God appointed them not to wrath but to salvation through the Lord Jesus who died for them.
section.thesis: Because the Day of the Lord will fall suddenly on a sleeping world but believers belong to the day, they are to stay awake, self-controlled, and clothed in the armor of faith, love, and hope, assured that God has appointed them not to wrath but to salvation through the Lord Jesus who died so that they might live with Him.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the Day arrives like a thief on those who cry peace and security; believers are sons of the light who watch, stay sober, and put on the breastplate of faith and love and the helmet of hope; and the ground of their assurance, that God appointed them to salvation and not to wrath through Christ who died so they would live with Him.

units.label: The Day comes like a thief
units.note: sudden judgment on a careless world

verses.text: Now about the times and seasons, brothers, we do not need to write to you.
For you are fully aware that the {{hemeraKyriou|Day of the Lord}} will come like a {{kleptes|thief}} in the night.
While people are saying, “Peace and {{asphaleia|security}},” destruction will come upon them suddenly, like {{odin|labor pains}} on a pregnant woman, and they will not escape.

units.label: But you are sons of the day

verses.text: But you, brothers, are not in the darkness so that this day should overtake you like a thief.
For you are all {{huios|sons}} of the light and sons of the day; we do not belong to the night or to the darkness.
So then, let us not sleep as the others do, but let us {{gregoreo|remain awake}} and {{nepho|sober}}.
For those who sleep, sleep at night, and those who get drunk, get drunk at night.
But since we belong to the day, let us be sober, putting on the {{thorax|breastplate}} of faith and love, and the {{perikephalaia|helmet}} of our hope of salvation.
For God has not appointed us to suffer {{orge|wrath}}, but to obtain {{soteria|salvation}} through our Lord Jesus Christ.
He died for us so that, whether we are awake or asleep, we may live together with Him.
Therefore encourage and {{oikodomeo|build}} one another up, just as you are already doing.

hemeraKyriou.gloss: The Day of the Lord, a phrase drawn from the prophets for the decisive day when God comes to judge and to save. Paul applies it to the return of the Lord Jesus. It is a fixed and certain day, but its timing is hidden, so the emphasis falls not on calculating when it comes but on being ready whenever it does.

kleptes.gloss: A thief. The Day comes like a thief in the night, unannounced and unexpected, catching the sleeping world off guard. The image is not that the Day is evil but that it is sudden; those who are alert are not surprised by a thief, while those who are asleep are caught unprepared.

asphaleia.gloss: Safety, security, a settled sense that all is well. The world cries peace and security precisely when destruction is nearest. The word exposes a false confidence, a spiritual sleep that mistakes calm for safety and so is caught defenseless when the Day breaks.

odin.gloss: A birth pang, the sudden and inescapable onset of labor. Destruction comes on the careless like labor pains on a pregnant woman: unavoidable once begun, and impossible to postpone. The picture stresses both the suddenness and the certainty of the coming judgment.

huios.gloss: A son, here in the Hebrew idiom sons of the light and sons of the day, meaning those who belong to the light and share its character. Believers are not merely told to act enlightened; they are children of the day by God's grace, and their conduct is to match the family to which they now belong.

gregoreo.gloss: To stay awake, to be watchful and alert. Because believers belong to the day, they are not to drift into the spiritual sleep of the world but to keep watch, living with the Lord's coming in view. Wakefulness here is not anxious date-watching but attentive, ready faith.

nepho.gloss: To be sober, clear-headed, self-controlled, the opposite of being drunk or dulled. Paul calls believers to a sober-minded steadiness that is not intoxicated by the world's pleasures or lulled by its false peace, but keeps a clear and disciplined grip on the truth as the Day approaches.

thorax.gloss: A breastplate, the armor that guards the heart and vital organs. Paul pictures faith and love as the breastplate of the Christian soldier. The believer facing the coming Day is not passive but armed, protected at the heart by trust in God and love for others.

perikephalaia.gloss: A helmet, the armor that guards the head. The hope of salvation is the helmet, the sure expectation of final deliverance that steadies the mind and keeps the believer standing. Faith, love, and hope together are the armor for those who wait for the Lord.

orge.gloss: Wrath, the settled righteous anger of God against sin, poured out on the Day of the Lord. Paul says God has not appointed His people to this wrath. The destruction that falls on the careless is not the destiny of those who are in Christ, for He has borne it in their place.

soteria.gloss: Salvation, deliverance, rescue. It is what God has appointed His people to obtain through the Lord Jesus Christ. Here salvation looks especially to the final day: to be saved from wrath and brought safely through to live forever with the Lord. It is God's appointment, not the believer's achievement.

oikodomeo.gloss: To build up, as one builds a house, used for the strengthening of fellow believers. Paul tells the church not only to encourage one another but to build one another up. The teaching about the Day is given for mutual construction, so that believers strengthen each other to keep watching and standing firm.

basic.context: Paul has just comforted the church about believers who have died. Now he answers a related question: when will the Lord come? He refuses to set dates. The Day of the Lord will arrive suddenly, like a thief at night, catching a careless world by surprise while it congratulates itself on peace and safety. But Christians are different. They belong to the light and the day, so they are to live awake, clear-headed, and armed with faith, love, and hope. Their deepest comfort is that God has not appointed them to suffer His wrath but to be saved through Jesus, who died for them so that they would live with Him.
basic.hermeneutics: This is not a passage for calculating the timing of the end. Paul deliberately turns from times and seasons to how believers should live now. The certainty is the coming of the Day and the safety of those in Christ; the response is watchfulness and self-control, not speculation. What the passage prescribes is a way of life, alert and sober and armed, grounded in the sure hope of salvation.
basic.originalLanguages: The hemera kyriou, the Day of the Lord, comes like a kleptes, a thief, while the world cries asphaleia, security, and is overtaken by destruction like odin, birth pangs. But believers are huios, sons, of the light, called to gregoreo, keep awake, and to nepho, be sober, putting on the thorax, breastplate, of faith and love and the perikephalaia, helmet, of hope. God has appointed them not to orge, wrath, but to soteria, salvation, so they are to oikodomeo, build, one another up.
basic.typology: The Day of the Lord takes up the prophets' theme of a decisive day of judgment and salvation, now centered on the return of Jesus. The armor of faith, love, and hope echoes God arming His people, and points to the fuller picture of the armor of God. The believer as a soldier who watches through the night looks to Christ, the faithful watchman who keeps His people to the end.
basic.christ: The whole passage rests on verse 10: He died for us so that we may live together with Him. Christ has borne the wrath that the Day would otherwise bring, so that those who are His are appointed not to wrath but to salvation. Whether awake or asleep, alive or fallen asleep in death, they will live with Him. The Christian faces the coming Day without terror because Jesus has already faced the judgment in their place.
basic.god: God is the judge whose Day will surely come, and He is the one who has appointed His people to salvation rather than wrath. He sets the times and seasons by His own authority, and He secures the destiny of those in Christ. The believer's confidence rests on God's appointment and God's gift, not on human readiness alone.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 24 records Jesus warning that His coming will be sudden, like a thief, and calling His people to watch. Romans 13 urges believers to wake from sleep and put on the armor of light. And Ephesians 6 unfolds the full armor of God for standing firm.
basic.oneStory: The prophets long spoke of the Day of the Lord, when God would come to judge evil and rescue His people. That Day now centers on the return of Jesus. Because He died and rose, His people are not appointed to the coming wrath but to salvation, and they wait for the Day awake and armed, building one another up until the King appears.

context.literary:
The passage is built on a series of sharp contrasts, and the grammar makes them audible. 'They' and 'you' stand against each other in verses 3 and 4: 'While people are saying, "Peace and security," destruction will come upon them... But you, brothers, are not in the darkness.' Then 'the others' and 'let us' in verse 6. Night and day, sleep and wakefulness, drunkenness and sobriety, darkness and light, wrath and salvation run through the section as paired opposites, and Paul places believers on one side of each pair and then urges them to live like it.

The movement has three beats. Verses 1 to 3 deal with timing and answer the question by declining to answer it, with a reminder of what the church already knows. Verses 4 to 8 turn from the world to the church, shifting from the third person plural to the first person plural, and move from indicative to imperative: 'you are sons of the light,' therefore 'let us remain awake and sober.' Verses 9 to 11 then give the reason the whole thing can be borne, an appointment of God and a death of Christ, and close with the same command that closed chapter 4, 'encourage,' now joined by 'build one another up.'

The section also has a visible inner shape in verses 5 to 8. Paul declares what the church is, 'sons of the light and sons of the day,' then what it must do, 'remain awake and sober,' then explains with a little proverb about the habits of the night, verse 7, then returns to the command with a picture of armor. The ordering is identity, duty, reason, equipment.

The passage begins with 'Now about the times and seasons,' the same sort of formula that opened a new topic in chapter 4, and it is paired with the previous passage as two halves of one answer. The first half told the church about the dead. This half tells the living how to wait.
context.historical:
The phrase 'times and seasons,' chronoi and kairoi, is the language of the disciples' question at the ascension, when Jesus replied that it was not for them to know the times or dates the Father had set by His own authority, Acts 1:7. Paul says the Thessalonians do not need a letter on the subject because they already know the main point, 'fully aware,' verse 2. Their earlier teaching, from the weeks Paul spent in the city, evidently included the saying that the Day comes like a thief. Jesus used that picture more than once, Matthew 24:43 and 44 and Luke 12:39 and 40, and the earliest Christians seem to have passed it around, since Peter and John echo it too, 2 Peter 3:10 and Revelation 16:15.

The cry of 'Peace and security' belonged to the public mood of the Roman Empire. The empire's own propaganda boasted of a world pacified and kept safe under Rome, and many scholars hear an echo of that in verse 3. Paul does not name Rome, and the text does not require that reading. What it does require is the Old Testament background that the prophets denounced the same slogan in Israel's own mouth: 'They dress the wound of My people with very little care, saying, "Peace, peace," when there is no peace at all,' Jeremiah 6:14, and Ezekiel 13:10 says the same of false prophets. The thief's night is an unwelcome visitor to a city that has comforted itself with a lie.

The images from daily life were all ones the Thessalonians knew. Nights in a Greek port city were marked by feasting and drinking, and the point of verse 7 is that no one expects to find drunkards at noon. Watchmen guarded city walls through the night, so staying awake and sober was the work of soldiers on duty. The labor pains of verse 3 are a picture the prophets used for the sudden onset of judgment, Isaiah 13:8, and for the pains of the new age, a thing that cannot be stopped once it begins.

For a church under pressure from neighbors, as chapters 1 to 3 show, the claim that God has not appointed them to wrath was no abstract doctrine. It spoke straight into persecution, and 1 Thessalonians 1:10 had already called Jesus the deliverer from the coming wrath.
context.canonical:
The Day of the Lord is one of the largest threads in the prophets. Amos met a people who longed for it and told them it would be darkness and not light, Amos 5:18 to 20. Isaiah says it comes as destruction from the Almighty, Isaiah 13:6, Joel 2:1 calls for the ram's horn to be blown because it is near, and Zephaniah 1:14 to 16 describes it as a day of wrath, of darkness and gloom, of horn blast and battle cry. Malachi 3:2 asks, 'who can endure the day of His coming?' and 4:1 speaks of a day burning like a furnace. Yet the prophets also saw salvation on that Day, as when Jeremiah 30:7 calls it a time of distress for Jacob 'but he will be saved out of it,' and Zechariah 14:5 has the Lord coming with all His holy ones.

The New Testament gives that day a face. The thief imagery comes from Jesus Himself, Matthew 24:42 to 44, and the comparison to Noah's day, when people carried on eating and drinking and were oblivious until the flood came, Matthew 24:37 to 39. Luke 21:34 to 36 warns that the day will spring suddenly like a snare, and tells the disciples to keep watch and pray. Peter and John bring the same note, 2 Peter 3:10 and Revelation 16:15, and in the second Thessalonian letter Paul himself will return to the subject to correct a false alarm, 2 Thessalonians 2:1 and 2.

The armor in verse 8 begins in Isaiah, where the Lord Himself puts on righteousness like a breastplate and the helmet of salvation on His head, Isaiah 59:17. Paul develops it into the fuller panoply of Ephesians 6:13 to 17, which swaps in other pieces. The imperative to wake from sleep and clothe oneself in the light of the coming day also appears in Romans 13:11 to 14, 'the night is nearly over; the day has drawn near.'

The assurance of verse 9, not wrath but salvation, finds its fullest statement in Romans 5:9, 'since we have now been justified by His blood, how much more shall we be saved from wrath through Him,' and in Romans 8:1, 'there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.'

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wanted to move a church from asking when to asking how. The question about dates is a natural one for a persecuted people, because it is really a question about how long the hardship will last. He answers by pointing out that the answer is deliberately held back, and by showing that what matters is the kind of people they are when the Day comes, whenever that is.

He also wanted the church to understand its own identity. 'You are all sons of the light and sons of the day' is stated as fact before it becomes a command. Paul does not say 'try to become people of the day.' He says they already are, and the commands to stay awake and sober flow from that. Obedience is the outworking of a status the church already has in Christ, not a way of obtaining it.

A third aim is to guard against two opposite errors at once. One is complacency, the kind of settled ease that the world shows when it says 'peace and security' and that believers can drift into. The other is fear, the dread that being caught at the wrong moment would cost them their salvation. Verses 9 and 10 settle that fear. Staying alert is for the sake of faithfulness, not to earn an exemption from wrath, since the appointment to salvation has already been made by God.

Finally, he gives the church a communal task, as at the end of chapter 4: encourage and build one another up. Watching for the Day is not a solitary spiritual exercise. It is done together, in a community that keeps each other awake.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
There is more command in this passage than in the one before it. The description is of the Day, which will come suddenly and without escape for those who say 'Peace and security,' and of believers' standing in the light. The commands are in the first person plural, which includes Paul: let us not sleep, let us remain awake, let us be sober, put on the breastplate and helmet, encourage and build one another up. What is prescribed is a posture of ordinary life, not a program of special acts.

That means the passage should be read as a charge to character and habits, not as a forecast to be mined. Staying awake does not mean staring at the sky, and sobriety is about clear thinking and self-command, not about asceticism. Paul's own picture of the breastplate and helmet shows that the waiting is active: the armor consists of faith, love and hope, which are the three marks Paul praised in 1:3 and which are put to work in daily life.

It is also important what the passage does not command. It does not tell believers to fear. It does not tell them to calculate. It does not tell them to withdraw from society to await the Day. Verse 10 explicitly says that whether we are awake or asleep, we live together with Him, which means that a believer's momentary failure of alertness does not undo the appointment of verse 9. The commands are real, but they are given to people who are already safe in Christ.

debates.question: What does 'whether we are awake or asleep' mean in verse 10?

views.label: Alive or dead at His coming
views.case: Verse 10 uses gregoreo, to be awake, and katheudo, to sleep. In chapter 4 Paul used koimaomai for death, but here he uses a different word. Even so, the dead and the living of chapter 4 sit just behind this verse, and that makes the pairing natural. On this view Paul is returning to his first question: whether alive or dead when He comes, believers live together with Him.

views.label: Spiritually alert or spiritually careless
views.case: In verses 6 and 7 the same katheudo meant moral drowsiness, and gregoreo meant alertness. Reading verse 10 in the same sense gives the result that even those who have grown careless are not cut off from the Lord, since He died for them. Some commentators find this too lax; others find it a deliberate and gracious paradox.

views.label: Both are meant
views.case: Paul may be deliberately reusing the words of verse 6 while pointing back to chapter 4, so that his readers hear the two senses together. The assurance covers the living, the dead and the lapsing alike.

debates.bearing: All three readings land on the same ground: the safety of the believer rests on Christ's death 'for us' and not on the believer's performance. The commands of verses 6 and 8 are urgent, and yet the promise of verse 10 stands over them.

debates.question: What is the wrath from which believers are exempt, and when?

views.label: Final eschatological condemnation
views.case: The wrath in 1:10, 2:16 and 5:9 is the settled judgment of God on sin at the last day. Romans 5:9 uses nearly the same language, 'saved from wrath through Him,' and Romans 8:1 says there is no condemnation for those in Christ. On this view verse 9 promises that no believer will face the judgment that falls on the world, and says nothing about whether the church passes through earthly trouble.

views.label: A coming time of tribulation judgments
views.case: Others take 'wrath' as the specific outpouring of divine anger that Revelation describes on the earth before Christ's return, and read verse 9, together with the 'rescue' of 1:10, as a promise that the church will be taken out before it. They note that 4:13 to 18 and 5:1 to 11 are placed together as a single movement.

views.label: Wrath as the day itself, from which believers are kept by Christ's presence
views.case: A third reading holds that the church lives through the age's troubles, as 3:3 says believers are destined for trials, but is preserved from the final wrath. It stresses that the Day of the Lord in the prophets includes both judgment and rescue, and that verse 9 pairs wrath with salvation, which in Paul's usage is largely about the last day.

debates.bearing: The text says plainly that wrath is not our appointment, and that is the load-bearing claim. How the church's exemption fits into a larger timetable of events is a separate question on which verse 9 is silent, and honest readers differ.

study.originalLanguages:
The phrase 'times and seasons,' chronoi kai kairoi, in verse 1 pairs the word for clock time with the word for a fitting or critical moment. Acts 1:7 uses the same pair in Jesus' answer to His disciples. The two words together cover every way a person might try to calculate the end, by duration or by occasion, and Paul says there is no need to write about either. The word for 'fully aware,' akribos, comes from a root meaning precision, and in verse 2 Paul teases them gently: they know with accuracy that the Day cannot be known.

In verse 3 the word for 'security,' asphaleia, means firmness, certainty, a thing that cannot be made to slip. It is the word Luke uses when he promises Theophilus the certainty of the things he has been taught, Luke 1:4. The slogan in the world's mouth borrows the vocabulary of confidence. The 'destruction' that falls, olethros, is the same noun that 2 Thessalonians 1:9 will describe as 'eternal destruction.' The suddenness is conveyed by aiphnidios, 'suddenly,' and the picture is intensified by odin, the pain of labor. Jesus used the same noun in Mark 13:8 for 'the beginning of birth pains.' A labor cannot be stopped once it starts, and it does not wait for the mother to be ready. The double negative ou me ekphygosin, 'they will not escape,' uses the same emphatic form as ou me phthasomen in 4:15, so the certainty of the judgment is stated as strongly as the certainty of the dead's priority.

Verse 5 says 'sons of the light and sons of the day.' The Hebrew way of speaking, 'son of,' marks belonging and character, as in 'sons of disobedience' in Ephesians 5:6. The Dead Sea community called themselves sons of light, but Paul's use here comes straight from the way Scripture speaks of those whose nature is shaped by what they belong to.

The pair of verbs in verse 6, gregoreo, 'remain awake,' and nepho, 'be sober,' belong together in the New Testament. The first is the word Jesus uses in Gethsemane, 'watch and pray,' Matthew 26:41, and the second means clear-headed, free from intoxication, as in 1 Peter 1:13 and 5:8. Paul says 'let us,' joining himself to the command.

In verse 9 the verb translated 'appointed' is etheto, from tithemi, 'to set or place.' God has set us toward salvation. The word translated 'obtain' in the phrase 'to obtain salvation' is peripoiesis, a word that means acquiring or possessing. It is related to the 'people for God's own possession' of 1 Peter 2:9. Salvation is spoken of as something gained, and the text hints that the gain is both ours and God's. Finally, 'build one another up' is oikodomeo, from oikos, house, the verb for construction, and is the word Paul uses in 1 Corinthians 8:1 and 14:4 for what love and edification do in the church.

typology.type: The night of the Passover and the flood, Exodus 12:29 and Matthew 24:37 to 39
typology.fulfillment: At midnight the Lord struck Egypt, Exodus 12:29, and in Noah's day people went on eating and drinking until the flood came and swept them away, Matthew 24:38 and 39. Both are nights in which judgment arrived on a world that was going about its business, while a protected household inside the ark or behind the blood stood safe. The Day of the Lord repeats the pattern on a larger scale. The Lord Jesus ties the two together by saying that the coming of the Son of Man will be as it was in the days of Noah. The escalation is that the final Day is universal and final, and the household that is safe is gathered under the blood of the Lamb, not a lamb's blood on a doorframe. The earlier events fall short in that both were local and both left a world behind to carry on.

During the plague of darkness Egypt was blind for three days, 'Yet all the Israelites had light in their dwellings,' Exodus 10:23. The people of God lived in the light while their neighbors lived in the dark. Paul's 'sons of the light and sons of the day' stands in that line, and so does Peter's description of believers called 'out of darkness into His marvelous light,' 1 Peter 2:9. In Christ the light is no longer a gift to one nation's tents but the life of a people drawn from every nation, and it belongs to them not because of a plague's boundary but because He is 'the light of the world,' John 8:12. The type is limited because the Goshen light was a sign that ended with the plague, whereas the light of the day belongs to believers permanently.

Isaiah shows the Lord putting on righteousness like a breastplate and the helmet of salvation, going out to rescue a people no human could help, Isaiah 59:16 and 17. Paul takes pieces of the Lord's own armor and puts them on His people, though he exchanges the pieces: faith and love for the breastplate, hope of salvation for the helmet. The fuller picture is in Ephesians 6:13 to 17. The correspondence shows that the believer fights with what God supplies, not with native resources. In Christ, who is the true Warrior, the armor is shared with the church, and the church's weapons are the virtues He produced in His own life. The type falls short because the Lord in Isaiah fights for a people who cannot, while the church is a people who stand alongside Him.

typology.type: Labor pains and the birth of a new age, Isaiah 13:8 and Romans 8:22
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah describes the Day of the LORD with the image of a woman in labor, terror and pain seizing those who face it, Isaiah 13:8. Paul draws on the same picture for the suddenness of the Day, and Jesus speaks of wars and earthquakes as 'the beginning of birth pains,' Mark 13:8. The image has two edges. Pain that cannot be stopped is a fearful thing to those unprepared, yet birth pains end in a birth. Romans 8:22 says that the whole creation groans in the pains of childbirth until the present time, and the thing being born is the freedom of the children of God. The Day of the Lord is therefore both a judgment and a delivery. The type is limited, because human labor ends in a child who must still grow, whereas this birth ends in a world made new.

study.christ:
The passage builds toward verse 10, and verse 10 is where Christ stands. 'He died for us so that, whether we are awake or asleep, we may live together with Him.' Everything before it prepares the ground and everything after it applies it.

Christ is the one who removes the wrath. The Day of the Lord in the prophets was a day of wrath, Zephaniah 1:15, and Paul does not deny that. What he says is that God 'has not appointed us to suffer wrath,' verse 9, and that the reason is the cross. Romans 5:9 says that we have been justified by His blood and will therefore be saved from wrath through Him, and 1 Thessalonians 1:10 calls Him 'Jesus our deliverer from the coming wrath.' The terror of the Day was met at Golgotha. At the cross the Son took what the Day would otherwise have brought, as Isaiah 53:5 and 10 describe the servant bearing the penalty. When a Christian faces the thought of judgment, the thought is not empty, because the judgment has already been borne by someone for him.

Christ is also the one in whom the Day becomes a day of light. In the prophets the Day was darkness, Amos 5:18, but in Christ the people of God are 'sons of the light and sons of the day.' He is the light of the world, John 8:12, and the dawn that Malachi 4:2 describes as the sun of righteousness rising with healing in its wings. The Day arrives to believers as sunrise, since they belong to the day and not the night.

Christ is the goal of the 'live together with Him' in verse 10. The word 'together,' hama, links this to 4:17 and 'always with the Lord.' The whole passage ends where chapter 4 ended, in His company. The two sections are one answer: whatever the Day brings, the believer is with Him.

The armor too is Christian in the deepest sense. Faith, love and hope are what the church offered in 1:3, and they are the virtues the Lord Himself showed. Isaiah 59:17 has the LORD in breastplate and helmet, and Christ is the one who fought and won, so that the church may be clothed in what He has made available, 'clothe yourselves with the Lord Jesus Christ,' Romans 13:14. We should not overpress the allegory by assigning each piece to a specific action of Jesus. The point is the big one: those who are in Christ wear what He has won.

There is also a contrast with the thief. Jesus warned that He would come like a thief, but the thief of verse 2 is not a Savior who steals, it is a Savior who arrives unannounced. The surprise falls on a world that did not watch. For those who do, the same coming is the arrival of the one they love, and they greet Him with the 'blessed hope' of Titus 2:13.
study.god:
God appears in this passage as the one who appoints. Verse 9 uses a verb of deliberate placing, 'God has not appointed us,' and it points to a decision made before any watchfulness of ours. The believer's destiny is not left to chance or to the performance of a given night. That is the doctrine of election being used for its proper purpose in Scripture, as a source of steadiness rather than anxiety, and Paul had already said in 1:4 that God had chosen them.

He is also the God who keeps His own counsel about time. 'Times and seasons' belong to Him alone. Jesus said the Father has set them by His own authority, Acts 1:7, and in Mark 13:32 that not even the Son knew the day or hour. Paul's refusal to speculate is therefore a form of reverence. The unknown date is not a defect in the revelation but a feature of a God who rules history and does not need to consult us about it.

He is the God of just wrath, and the passage will not allow that to be softened. Destruction comes upon those who say 'peace and security,' and they will not escape. This is the divine anger that the prophets proclaimed, not a human outburst of temper but the settled opposition of a holy God to what destroys His creation. Paul assumes that readers know it is real. It is because wrath is real that verse 9 is such good news.

He is, at the same time, the God who saves. The pairing in verse 9 of 'wrath' and 'salvation' is the structure of the gospel. The same God holds both, and the cross is where they meet. 'Through our Lord Jesus Christ' says that God provides the way of escape in the person of His Son and does not leave the matter to the sinner's ingenuity.

He is also the God who arms His people. Isaiah 59:17 has Him wear the breastplate and helmet; here He gives pieces of that armor to a church. It is the pattern of the whole Bible that God's gifts to His people are shares in His own character and strength.

There is a tension to hold. God commands watchfulness and also assures the believer that his sleeping or waking does not change the outcome. The passage never resolves this by diluting either side. It lets the command stand in full force and the promise stand in full force, and it trusts the believer to live between them: awake because he is safe, not awake in order to be safe. For worship that is the posture of a people who sing at dawn.

crossReferences.note: Jesus's own teaching on the thief. He says keep watch because you do not know the day, and compares the Day to a homeowner who would have stayed awake had he known when the thief was coming. Paul's picture in verse 2 is plainly taken from this teaching, though his readers already knew it from his oral instruction.

Jesus warns that hearts weighed down by dissipation, drunkenness and the worries of life will be caught by that day like a snare, and tells His people to keep watch and pray. The link with 'sober' and 'those who get drunk, get drunk at night' in 5:7 is close, and the surprise is again universal.

Paul tells the Romans that the hour has come to wake from slumber, that the night is nearly over and the day has drawn near, and that they must put on the armor of light and clothe themselves with the Lord Jesus. It is the same call as 1 Thessalonians 5:4 to 8, written to a different church.

The fuller list of the armor of God, with belt, breastplate of righteousness, shoes, shield of faith, helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit. Here Paul gives a different set of pieces from 1 Thessalonians 5:8, which shows that the armor is an image he reworks, not a fixed list.

The source of the picture. The Lord Himself puts on righteousness like a breastplate and the helmet of salvation. Paul takes the Divine Warrior's armor and shows it handed to His people, who are to fight with what He provides.

A warning to those who longed for the Day of the LORD that it would be darkness and not light, with the picture of a man fleeing a lion and meeting a bear. It supplies the prophetic background to the sudden catastrophe of verse 3 and to Paul's insistence that believers are not in darkness.

The prophet condemns those who say 'Peace, peace,' when there is no peace at all. The slogan of 1 Thessalonians 5:3 is the same false comfort, and the destruction that follows has the same suddenness. Jeremiah shows that the lie of security is an old one.

'Since we have now been justified by His blood, how much more shall we be saved from wrath through Him!' It is the doctrinal basis of 1 Thessalonians 5:9. The appointment to salvation is set within the work of the cross and is stated as a settled consequence of justification.

The letter opens with a church that turned from idols to serve the living God and to await His Son from heaven, Jesus our deliverer from the coming wrath. Chapter 5 returns to the same theme at the close and gives the practical manner of waiting.

Jesus tells His disciples it is not for them to know times or dates that the Father has set by His own authority. Paul's 'times and seasons' in verse 1 uses the same pair of words, and his refusal to speculate follows the Lord's own refusal.

The signs of the end are called 'the beginning of birth pains.' The same word for labor pains appears in 1 Thessalonians 5:3, and together they show that the image is a Christian way of speaking about the sudden onset and inevitability of the coming age.

The great Day of the LORD is near, a day of wrath, trouble, darkness and gloom, a day of horn blast and battle cry. It is one of the most vivid prophetic descriptions of what Paul means by the Day, and it explains why the promise of verse 9 is such a relief.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a created order in which light is separated from darkness, Genesis 1:3 to 5, and the first light is called good. Sin brought darkness into the human story, in the sense of ignorance of God, hidden deeds and the shadow of death, and the whole of Scripture is the account of a God who reverses that. The prophets looked toward a Day on which He would act decisively, to judge wickedness and to rescue His people. Some hearers longed for it and were warned that they were not ready. Others lived under it as a threat.

This passage places that Day inside the gospel. The story of the Old Testament had left a question: who can stand on that Day? Malachi 3:2 asks it outright. Paul's answer in 1 Thessalonians 5 is that those who are in Christ will stand, because the Lord Jesus died for them and God has appointed them to salvation. What had been dread in Amos is, for the people of Christ, a coming sunrise.

The passage also answers a puzzle from the story of Israel. The people of God had so often been asleep, in the wilderness, in the time of the judges, in the long exile, that a call to wakefulness could seem a hopeless one. Paul says the church is the people of the day, which means the life of the new age has already begun in them. They live in the light that the end will make plain. The armor of faith, love and hope is the equipment for the interval between the first coming and the second, an interval that the whole New Testament treats as a watch.

Looking forward, the story ends not with a thief in the night but with a day that has no night. Revelation 21:25 says that its gates will never be shut by day, and there will be no night there, and Revelation 22:5 says they will not need the light of a lamp or the sun, for the Lord God will give them light. The long contrast of this passage, night against day, will be resolved. The wrath that threatens the world will have been spent, the sleepers will be awake, and the people who held on to faith, love and hope in the dark will find that they have walked all the way into morning.

sermon.title: Sons of the Day Stay Awake and Sober: 1 Thessalonians 5:6-11, Part 1
sermon.why: Piper shows how belonging to the day shapes the way believers live, calling them to wakeful, sober faith while grounding their assurance in verses 9 and 10, that God appointed them to salvation and Christ died so they would live with Him.

quiz.q: How does Paul describe the coming of the Day of the Lord?

options.text: It comes suddenly, like a thief in the night, on a careless world.
options.note: Verse 2 says the Day comes like a thief in the night.

options.text: It comes only after clear signs everyone can calculate.
options.note: Paul refuses date-setting; the Day is sudden and its hour hidden.

options.text: It comes gently and gradually, with plenty of warning.
options.note: The image is sudden and inescapable, like labor pains.

options.text: It will never actually come.
options.note: The Day is certain; the point is readiness for it.

quiz.q: Why does Paul say the Day will not overtake believers like a thief?

options.text: Because they are sons of the light and the day, not of the darkness.
options.note: Verses 4 and 5 ground this in their identity as children of the day.

options.text: Because they will know the exact date in advance.
options.note: They are ready by watching, not by knowing the date.

options.text: Because they will never have to face that Day.
options.note: They do meet the Day, but as those prepared, not surprised.

options.text: Because they are naturally better than other people.
options.note: It is God's grace making them sons of light, not native merit.

quiz.q: What armor does Paul tell believers to put on?

options.text: The breastplate of faith and love, and the helmet of the hope of salvation.
options.note: Verse 8 names faith, love, and hope as the believer's armor.

options.text: Only the helmet, since hope is all that matters.
options.note: Paul names faith, love, and hope together, not hope alone.

options.text: Weapons to take vengeance on the world.
options.note: The armor is faith, love, and hope for standing firm, not for vengeance.

options.text: No armor at all; believers simply wait passively.
options.note: Paul calls them to be actively armed and alert.

quiz.q: To what has God appointed His people, according to verse 9?

options.text: Not to wrath, but to obtain salvation through the Lord Jesus Christ.
options.note: Verse 9 states the appointment plainly: salvation, not wrath.

options.text: To earn their salvation by staying awake.
options.note: Watchfulness matters, but salvation is God's appointment and gift.

options.text: To suffer the same destruction as the world.
options.note: The opposite: they are appointed to salvation, not wrath.

options.text: To an uncertain outcome they cannot know.
options.note: Their destiny is settled in Christ, so it is a sure hope.

quiz.q: What is the ground of the believer's confidence before the coming Day?

options.text: Christ died for us so that we may live together with Him.
options.note: Verse 10 grounds everything in Jesus dying so His people would live with Him.

options.text: The strength of our own watchfulness and effort.
options.note: Watchfulness flows from grace; the ground is Christ's death.

options.text: The hope that God will overlook sin on that Day.
options.note: God does not overlook sin; Christ bore the wrath for it.

options.text: The chance that the Day may never arrive.
options.note: The Day is certain; the comfort is that Christ died so we live with Him.

questions: The world says peace and security while the Day draws near. Where are you tempted to trade real readiness for a false sense that all is well?
Paul calls believers to stay awake and sober. What does spiritual sleep or dullness look like in your life right now, and what would wakefulness look like instead?
Faith, love, and hope are the Christian's armor. Which of these feels weakest in you at the moment, and how might you put it on this week?
God has appointed you not to wrath but to salvation through Christ who died for you. How does that settled destiny change the way you face the future?
Paul says to encourage and build one another up. Who could you strengthen this week with the hope that we will live together with the Lord?

translationNotes.note: The Day of the Lord renders a phrase the prophets used for God's decisive day of judgment and salvation, here applied to the return of the Lord Jesus.
Sons of the light and sons of the day is a Hebrew idiom meaning those who belong to and share the character of the light, not merely those who behave well.
Whether we are awake or asleep echoes the language of sleep for death from the previous passage, so the promise covers believers living and dead alike.
